title: "Randomization Tests with Your Own Test Statistic"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      fig.align = "center")
render_start = Sys.time()
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

Every EDI inference class has a randomization test built in, but each one tests
with its own statistic: a mean difference, a regression coefficient, a log hazard
ratio. Sometimes the statistic you want is different. You may care about the
median rather than the mean, about the whole distribution rather than a location
shift, or about a covariate-adjusted contrast that no built-in class computes.
`InferenceRandCustom` runs a randomization test, and for continuous outcomes a
randomization confidence interval, on any statistic you write as an R function.

The reference distribution comes from the design you actually ran. If the trial
used matched pairs, the test redraws assignments within those pairs. If it used
rerandomization, it redraws only assignments that pass the same balance criterion.
It does not shuffle treatment labels freely, which would be the right reference
distribution only for a completely randomized design.

This article assumes you know the four steps of an EDI analysis (design, assign,
record responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html) or the
[continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html). If you need more than a test and
an interval, such as a standard error, a bootstrap or your own design, see
[Extending EDI](extending-edi.html), which shows how to write a full inference
class.

## What the test does

Write $y_i(1)$ and $y_i(0)$ for subject $i$'s potential outcomes under treatment
and control, and $w$ for the vector of treatment assignments. The randomization
test checks the **sharp null hypothesis**

$$H_0: y_i(1) = y_i(0) + \delta \quad \text{for every subject } i,$$

with $\delta = 0$ by default. "Sharp" means the hypothesis fixes every subject's
missing potential outcome, not just an average. If treatment does nothing at all,
each subject's response would have been the same under any assignment. So under
$H_0$ you can compute what your statistic $T(y, w)$ would have been under any
assignment the design could have produced, using only the data you observed.

The test then:

1. computes $T$ on the observed data;
2. draws `r` new assignment vectors $w^{(1)}, \dots, w^{(r)}$ from the design's own
   randomization mechanism, and computes $T$ on each, holding the responses fixed
   at their values under $H_0$;
3. reports how extreme the observed $T$ is in that reference distribution.

The default two-sided p-value doubles the smaller tail:
$\min\{1, 2\min(\hat P(T_0 \ge t), \hat P(T_0 \le t))\}$ over the draws $T_0$, with a
floor of $2/B$, where $B$ is the number of draws on which the statistic is finite
($B = r$ unless some draws are dropped; see Pitfalls). The test is valid, meaning it rejects a true $H_0$ at most at the
nominal rate up to Monte Carlo error, for **any** statistic you choose, because
validity comes from the randomization and not from a model. The choice of
statistic affects only power: how often the test rejects when $H_0$ is false.

The sharp null is a stronger statement than "the average effect is zero." A
treatment that helps some subjects and harms others, with zero average effect,
violates the sharp null, and a test of it can reject in that situation. Read a
small p-value as evidence that the treatment changed some outcomes, in the
direction your statistic is sensitive to.

## The statistic function

You pass a function of three arguments, `(y, w, dead)`, that returns one number:

- `y`: the response vector, one entry per subject, in the order the subjects were
  added to the design.
- `w`: a 0/1 treatment vector of the same length. On the observed data it is the
  actual assignment; in the reference draws it is a redrawn one.
- `dead`: the event indicator for survival outcomes (1 = event, 0 = censored). For
  other response types it is passed as a vector of 1s and you can ignore it.

EDI calls the function as `fn(y, w, dead)`, so it must accept all three arguments
even if it uses only two. Write `function(y, w, dead)` or `function(y, w, ...)`;
`function(y, w)` is rejected when the object is created, with "custom_randomization_statistic_function
must accept three arguments (y, w, dead) or `...`; it has 2."

The function is called once on the observed data, which is what
`compute_estimate()` returns, and once per reference draw.

## A first example: difference in medians on a matched-pair design

Here is a trial of 60 subjects with a right-skewed outcome (for example, length of
hospital stay). The subjects were paired on two baseline covariates and treatment
was assigned at random within each pair, using `DesignFixedBinaryMatch`.

```{r pairs-data}
set.seed(20261117)
n = 60
X = data.frame(age = rnorm(n, 50, 10), severity = rnorm(n))

des = DesignFixedBinaryMatch$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des$get_w()

y = exp(1 + 0.02 * (X$age - 50) + 0.4 * X$severity + rnorm(n, sd = 0.6)) - 0.8 * w
des$add_all_subject_responses(y)
```

With a skewed outcome, the difference in medians is less sensitive to a few very
long stays than the difference in means:

```{r median-stat}
median_diff = function(y, w, dead) median(y[w == 1]) - median(y[w == 0])

inf_med = InferenceRandCustom$new(des, custom_randomization_statistic_function = median_diff)
inf_med$compute_estimate()

inf_med$set_seed(1)
inf_med$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
```

`set_seed()` fixes the randomization draws so the p-value is reproducible (see
[Reproducibility](reproducibility.html)). `r` is the number of draws; the
[speed section](#speed) below discusses how many you need.

### Checking that the draws follow the design

The statistic sees each redrawn `w`, so a wrapper that records them shows what
the reference distribution is built from. On this design every draw should
assign exactly one subject of each pair to treatment:

```{r check-draws}
pair_id = des$get_block_ids()
seen = list()
recording_stat = function(y, w, dead) {
  seen[[length(seen) + 1]] <<- w
  median_diff(y, w, dead)
}
inf_check = InferenceRandCustom$new(des, custom_randomization_statistic_function = recording_stat)
inf_check$set_seed(1)
invisible(inf_check$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 200, show_progress = FALSE))

length(seen)                     # the observed assignment plus 200 draws
all(vapply(seen, function(w) all(tapply(w, pair_id, sum) == 1), logical(1)))
```

Every draw respects the pairs. A naive permutation test, which shuffles the 60
labels freely, would have split many pairs into two treated or two control
subjects, which this design can never do.

You can also look at the reference distribution itself.
`approximate_randomization_distribution_beta_hat_T()` returns the `r` values of the
statistic under $H_0$; with the same seed, they are the draws the p-value above
was computed from:

```{r null-hist}
inf_med$set_seed(1)
t0 = inf_med$approximate_randomization_distribution_beta_hat_T(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
hist(t0, breaks = 40, main = "Difference in medians under the sharp null",
     xlab = "statistic", col = "grey85", border = "white")
abline(v = inf_med$compute_estimate(), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

## Shifted nulls and a confidence interval

For a continuous outcome you can test a nonzero $\delta$: the sharp null that
treatment adds exactly $\delta$ to every subject's response. EDI subtracts
$\delta$ from the observed treated responses to recover the control outcomes, then
adds $\delta$ back to whichever subjects each draw assigns to treatment, and
computes your statistic on that:

```{r delta-pvals}
deltas = c(-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5)
pvals = vapply(deltas, function(d) {
  inf_med$set_seed(1)
  inf_med$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, delta = d, show_progress = FALSE)
}, numeric(1))
data.frame(delta = deltas, p_value = pvals)
```

The set of $\delta$ values that are not rejected at level $\alpha$ is a
$1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for the additive effect.
`compute_rand_confidence_interval()` finds its endpoints by bisection:

```{r median-ci}
inf_med$set_seed(1)
inf_med$compute_rand_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05, r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
```

Three things to know about this interval:

- **It is an interval for $\delta$, on the response scale, whatever your statistic
  measures.** The statistic only decides which $\delta$ values look implausible.
  A t statistic, a mean difference and ten times a mean difference all give the
  same interval. The interval assumes the additive model in $H_0$: a constant
  shift for every subject.
- **The statistic must respond to the shift.** As $\delta$ moves away from the
  truth, the observed statistic should move steadily toward one tail of the
  reference distribution. Location statistics (differences in means, medians,
  trimmed means) do. A statistic that ignores location, such as a difference in
  variances, cannot be inverted this way.
- **Each step of the search reruns all `r` draws.** The interval costs a few dozen
  p-value evaluations. Keep the statistic cheap (see [Speed](#speed)).

The search starts from the observed difference in means and its standard error,
not from your statistic's value, so the statistic can be on any scale.

## A statistic that uses covariates

The statistic may use any information that does not depend on the treatment
assignment, such as baseline covariates. Covariates are fixed under the sharp null,
so using them does not affect validity, and a statistic that removes the outcome
variation the covariates explain can have much more power.

A simple choice is the difference in means of the residuals from regressing the
outcome on the covariates alone, not on treatment. The fitted values are a
fixed linear function of `y` (the hat matrix), so precompute that matrix once,
outside the statistic:

```{r rerand-data}
set.seed(20261118)
n = 80
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n))

des_rr = DesignFixedRerandomization$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous",
                                        prop_acceptable = 0.1, verbose = FALSE)
des_rr$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_rr$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des_rr$get_w()
y = 2 * X$x1 + 1.5 * X$x2 - X$x3 + 0.5 * w + rnorm(n)
des_rr$add_all_subject_responses(y)
```

`DesignFixedRerandomization` with `prop_acceptable = 0.1` uses the best-balanced
of 10 candidate assignments; the randomization test redraws each assignment under
the same rule.

```{r resid-stat}
Z = cbind(1, as.matrix(X))
H = Z %*% solve(crossprod(Z), t(Z))      # hat matrix for y ~ x1 + x2 + x3

resid_diff = function(y, w, dead) {
  e = y - drop(H %*% y)
  mean(e[w == 1]) - mean(e[w == 0])
}
mean_diff = function(y, w, dead) mean(y[w == 1]) - mean(y[w == 0])

inf_res = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_rr, custom_randomization_statistic_function = resid_diff)
inf_raw = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_rr, custom_randomization_statistic_function = mean_diff)

ci = rbind(
  residualized = { inf_res$set_seed(1); inf_res$compute_rand_confidence_interval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE) },
  unadjusted   = { inf_raw$set_seed(1); inf_raw$compute_rand_confidence_interval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE) }
)
cbind(ci, width = ci[, 2] - ci[, 1])
```

Both intervals are valid, and both are intervals for the same additive effect.
The residualized statistic gives a narrower one because it removes the part of
the outcome variation that the covariates explain.

Two rules for statistics like this one:

- Compute anything that depends on `y` **inside** the function. Under a shifted
  null, `y` changes from draw to draw, so residualizing the observed `y` once in
  advance would be wrong. Only quantities that do not involve `y` or `w`, like `H`
  here, can be precomputed.
- Never let the statistic use the **observed** assignment, for example by
  capturing `des$get_w()` or group means computed from it. The statistic must
  depend on the assignment only through its `w` argument; otherwise the reference
  draws no longer represent what would have happened under another assignment.

## A statistic for any change in distribution

A statistic does not have to be signed. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between
the treated and control outcome distributions, the largest vertical gap between
their empirical distribution functions, picks up a change in spread or shape as
well as a shift. It is never negative, and only large values are evidence against
$H_0$. For a statistic like that, the default two-sided p-value, which doubles the
smaller tail, is wrong: pass `alternative = "greater"` to get the upper-tail
p-value.

Here treatment leaves the median alone but makes the outcome more variable:

```{r ks-data}
set.seed(20261119)
n = 80
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n))
des_ks = DesignFixedBernoulli$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
des_ks$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_ks$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des_ks$get_w()
y = rnorm(n, sd = ifelse(w == 1, 2.5, 1))
des_ks$add_all_subject_responses(y)
```

```{r ks-stat}
ks_stat = function(y, w, dead) {
  grid = sort(y)
  max(abs(ecdf(y[w == 1])(grid) - ecdf(y[w == 0])(grid)))
}
inf_ks = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_ks, custom_randomization_statistic_function = ks_stat)
inf_ks$compute_estimate()

inf_ks$set_seed(1)
inf_ks$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, alternative = "greater", show_progress = FALSE)

inf_mean = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_ks, custom_randomization_statistic_function = mean_diff)
inf_mean$set_seed(1)
inf_mean$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The distribution statistic detects the change; the mean difference, which looks
only for a shift, does not. There is no confidence interval for the KS statistic,
because it does not measure a location shift (see the previous section).

`alternative = "less"` gives the lower-tail p-value, for a statistic where only
small values are evidence against $H_0$.

## Using the design's structure in the statistic

Any statistic gives a valid test, but a statistic that matches the design's
structure is usually more powerful. The next trial uses the Kapelner-Krieger
sequential matching design (`DesignSeqOneByOneKK14`), which pairs each arriving
subject with a similar earlier subject when it can and leaves the rest in a
"reservoir" (see [Matching on the Fly](matching-on-the-fly.html)).

```{r kk-data}
set.seed(20261117)
n = 60
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n))
des_kk = DesignSeqOneByOneKK14$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
for (t in seq_len(n)) {
  w_t = des_kk$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X[t, , drop = FALSE])
  des_kk$add_one_subject_response(t, 1.5 * X$x1[t] + X$x2[t] + 0.5 * w_t + rnorm(1))
}
m = des_kk$get_block_ids()               # 0 = reservoir, k > 0 = pair k
table(ifelse(m == 0, "reservoir", "matched"))
```

The randomization test on this design keeps the matched pairs that the trial
formed and redraws the assignments within them. So a statistic can use the pair
labels `m`, which are fixed, together with the redrawn `w`. This one averages the
treated-minus-control difference within each pair, which removes the between-pair
variation that matching created, and ignores the reservoir for simplicity:

```{r kk-stats}
pair_diff = function(y, w, dead) {
  matched = m > 0
  signed = ifelse(w[matched] == 1, y[matched], -y[matched])
  mean(tapply(signed, m[matched], sum))
}

inf_pair = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_kk, custom_randomization_statistic_function = pair_diff)
inf_naive = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_kk, custom_randomization_statistic_function = mean_diff)

ci_kk = rbind(
  pair_differences = { inf_pair$set_seed(1); inf_pair$compute_rand_confidence_interval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE) },
  mean_difference  = { inf_naive$set_seed(1); inf_naive$compute_rand_confidence_interval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE) }
)
cbind(ci_kk, width = ci_kk[, 2] - ci_kk[, 1])
```

Both intervals come from the same design-based reference distribution and both are
valid. The pair-difference statistic gives the narrower interval because it uses the
matching. The built-in `InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik` goes further and combines the
pairs with the reservoir; your own statistic is useful when you want something it
does not compute.

## Other response types

The randomization test works for every response type. The statistic receives the
responses on their own scale: 0/1 for incidence, the raw counts for count
outcomes, the proportions for proportion outcomes, and the observed times plus the
event indicator `dead` for survival outcomes. For example, the difference in crude
event rates (events per unit of follow-up time) for a survival outcome with
right-censoring:

```{r survival}
set.seed(20261120)
n = 80
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n))
des_surv = DesignFixedBernoulli$new(n = n, response_type = "survival", verbose = FALSE)
des_surv$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_surv$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des_surv$get_w()
event_time = rexp(n, rate = exp(-0.7 * w))
follow_up = runif(n, 0.5, 3)
censored = event_time > follow_up
des_surv$add_all_subject_responses(
  ys   = ifelse(censored, NA, event_time),
  y_Ls = ifelse(censored, follow_up, NA),
  y_Rs = ifelse(censored, Inf, NA)
)

rate_diff = function(y, w, dead) {
  sum(dead[w == 1]) / sum(y[w == 1]) - sum(dead[w == 0]) / sum(y[w == 0])
}
inf_surv = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_surv, custom_randomization_statistic_function = rate_diff)
inf_surv$compute_estimate()
inf_surv$set_seed(1)
inf_surv$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
```

A nonzero `delta` shifts the treated responses on a scale that depends on the
response type (under the default `transform_responses = "none"`). EDI removes the
shift from the observed treated responses and re-imposes it on each draw's treated
responses on that same scale, and your statistic always sees the responses on their
own scale:

- **continuous**: additive, $y_i(1) = y_i(0) + \delta$ (the section above);
- **survival**: $\delta$ is a log time ratio, $y_i(1) = y_i(0)\,e^{\delta}$, with
  censoring times scaled alike and `dead` unchanged.
  `compute_rand_confidence_interval()` returns an interval for $\delta$;
  exponentiate its bounds for an interval for the time ratio $e^{\delta}$;
- **count**: $\delta$ is a log rate ratio (treated counts multiplied by
  $e^{\delta}$, then rounded);
- **proportion**: $\delta$ is a shift on the logit scale;
- **incidence**: a nonzero `delta` is refused.

`transform_responses = "log"` or `"logit"` picks the multiplicative or logit-scale
shift explicitly. The randomization interval is refused for incidence, count and
proportion responses, because its bounds would not be on the scale of the
statistic's raw-scale estimate; there, use the p-value at the `delta` you want to
test. For an effect
estimate with an interval on those outcomes, use the matching built-in class from
the cookbooks ([incidence](cookbook-incidence.html), [count](cookbook-count.html),
[proportion](cookbook-proportion.html), [survival](cookbook-survival.html),
[ordinal](cookbook-ordinal.html)).

## Speed {#speed}

The cost of a test is about `r` calls to your statistic, and a confidence interval
costs a few dozen tests. The statistic is called in a loop in your R session, so
setting `num_cores` does not split its calls across workers. Three things help:

- **Choose `r` for the precision you need.** The Monte Carlo standard error of a
  p-value near $p$ is about $\sqrt{p(1-p)/r}$. With 1,000 draws and a p-value near
  0.05, that is about 0.007. For a final report near a decision threshold, use
  several thousand draws.
- **Keep the statistic cheap.** Precompute everything that depends on neither `y`
  nor `w` (like the hat matrix above) and use vectorized base R inside. A
  statistic that fits a model on each call, such as `lm()` or `glm()`, is many
  times slower than the matrix product used above.
- **Write it in C++.** `custom_randomization_statistic_cpp` takes C++ source
  defining a function of `(NumericVector y, IntegerVector w)`, or
  `(NumericVector y, IntegerVector w, IntegerVector dead)`, that returns a
  `double`. EDI compiles it with `Rcpp::cppFunction()` when the object is created,
  which takes a few seconds and needs a C++ compiler. The source must hold exactly
  one function, the statistic: `cppFunction()` adds its own `// [[Rcpp::export]]`
  tag to the first function it finds, so a helper function placed before the
  statistic (even a forward declaration) is taken as the statistic and rejected, and
  an `// [[Rcpp::export]]` line of your own makes the compile fail. Put helper code in
  a lambda inside the statistic. For example:

```{r cpp-stat}
mean_diff_cpp = "
double mean_diff(Rcpp::NumericVector y, Rcpp::IntegerVector w) {
  double s1 = 0, s0 = 0; int n1 = 0, n0 = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < y.size(); i++) {
    if (w[i] == 1) { s1 += y[i]; n1++; } else { s0 += y[i]; n0++; }
  }
  return s1 / n1 - s0 / n0;
}"
inf_cpp = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_rr, custom_randomization_statistic_cpp = mean_diff_cpp)
inf_cpp$set_seed(1)
inf_cpp$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
inf_raw$set_seed(1)
inf_raw$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The two versions agree. Supply either `custom_randomization_statistic_function`
or `custom_randomization_statistic_cpp`, not both. For a simple statistic like
this one the R version is already fast; C++ pays off when the statistic loops
over subjects in a way base R cannot vectorize.

## Pitfalls

**A statistic that ignores the design is still valid, but can lose power.** The
reference distribution always comes from the design, so a statistic that knows
nothing about the pairs or blocks still gives a test with the right size. It just
may not use the precision the design bought, as the pair-difference example shows.

**Draws where the statistic is not finite are dropped.** If the function returns
`NA`, `NaN` or `Inf` on some draws, EDI drops them and computes the p-value from the
rest, without a warning. Here is a subgroup statistic for a subgroup of six
subjects, with treatment assigned by coin flip:

```{r na-stat}
set.seed(20261121)
n = 40
X = data.frame(female = rep(c(1, 0), c(6, 34)), x1 = rnorm(n))
des_sub = DesignFixedBernoulli$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
des_sub$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_sub$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des_sub$get_w()
des_sub$add_all_subject_responses(0.5 * w + rnorm(n))

subgroup_diff = function(y, w, dead) {
  s = X$female == 1
  mean(y[s & w == 1]) - mean(y[s & w == 0])     # NaN if no one in the subgroup is treated (or all are)
}
inf_sub = InferenceRandCustom$new(des_sub, custom_randomization_statistic_function = subgroup_diff)
inf_sub$set_seed(1)
t0 = inf_sub$approximate_randomization_distribution_beta_hat_T(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
mean(!is.finite(t0))                             # share of draws dropped
```

Dropping draws changes the reference distribution: the p-value now conditions on
the draws where the statistic exists. Check this share for any statistic that can
fail, and prefer a statistic that is defined for every assignment the design can
produce. If fewer than 10 draws, or fewer than 10% of `r`, give a finite value,
the p-value is `NA`.

**Return exactly one number.** A statistic that returns a vector of any other
length is an error ("the custom statistic ... must return one number"), raised on
the observed data before any draw.

**Pass `alternative = "greater"` for a non-negative statistic.** Squared
differences, absolute values, distances and chi-square-type statistics only signal
departures from $H_0$ in their upper tail. The default two-sided p-value counts
the lower tail as evidence too.

**Use a location statistic for confidence intervals.** The interval inverts an
additive shift, so it needs a statistic that moves steadily with the shift, and
it is only meaningful for continuous responses.
